articles.title: The hidden ways insects support animal life—from habitat to health—go way beyond being food
articles.dek: by Eliza Grames, Chris Elphick, Rob Cooke, The Conversation
paragraphs: by Eliza Grames, Chris Elphick, Rob Cooke, The Conversation

There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth , and they play highly diverse roles in sustaining the natural world. Insects provide many well-known benefits—what scientists often call "ecosystem services." For example, you can thank a bee or a hoverfly for pollinating wildflowers and agricultural crops , or credit dung beetles for decomposing manure and other waste materials.

Reports of rapid declines in insect abundance and biomass over the past decade have raised concerns about potential reductions in pollination , decomposition and other insect-provided services . Researchers have also noted that declines in insects could mean a change in the food supply for insectivores such as birds and bats.

In response to these concerns, a working group emerged as part of a Research Coordination Network on the Status of Insects . This international group of 21 researchers , including us , met via Zoom for a year and a half to discuss what declines in insects might mean for vertebrates—from birds to bats to bilbies .
What emerged from those discussions was a clear picture—insects are so much more than just food, and vertebrates rely on insects for everything from habitats to protection to health .
Insects can be ecosystem engineers, meaning they create and maintain habitats for other species.

Termites and ants build massive structures below and above ground that are used by many other species. Termite nests, for example, serve as climate-controlled spots for reptiles to lay eggs and for parrots to nest . In dry regions, some frogs live inside ant nests to take advantage of the humid conditions, masking themselves in pheromones to evade detection by their ant hosts.

The soil surrounding termite mounds also provides good conditions for species such as naked mole rats and aardvarks to make their burrows. Ant nests concentrate nutrients that enhance plant growth, thereby creating good grazing habitat for species like gazelles .
You probably don't usually think of something as small as a beetle as a protector, or of a wasp as a bodyguard. But vertebrates rely on insects for defense, even against other vertebrates.

For example, horned lizards turn chemicals from ants into a toxic, blood-spurting defense to ward off predators such as big cats. Poisonous frogs similarly get their toxicity from the chemical compounds found in insects they eat , as do some birds and snakes , which store toxins from ants and beetles as part of their defensive strategy.

Many birds will deliberately nest near wasp nests so the threat of being stung deters potential predators. Some vertebrates even mimic insects to avoid getting eaten, such as young songbirds in the Amazon that move their heads to look like fuzzy caterpillars —which they resemble—when predators are nearby.

Many insects, not just dung beetles, remove waste from ecosystems. By decomposing carcasses and dung, insects likely reduce disease transmission among wild vertebrates. For example, by tunneling through and burying dung, they make it an unsuitable place for parasites to live .

Certain mosquito species have gotten a bad reputation for transmitting diseases, including malaria, but other insects help control their populations. In their larval stage, dragonflies are fierce aquatic predators that eat mosquito larvae .

articles.title: Different text genres help doctoral students adapt their writing to reach new readers
articles.dek: An academic abstract, a blog post and a public outreach article all place different demands on the writer.
paragraphs: An academic abstract, a blog post and a public outreach article all place different demands on the writer. Readers' prior knowledge varies, as does the purpose of the text and what needs explaining. Mastering one kind of text therefore does not automatically mean being able to write another.

Researchers need to be able to write for both colleagues and people outside academia. But how do they learn to write for new audiences? A study from Chalmers shows how working with different text genres simultaneously can help doctoral students learn to adapt their writing to new contexts.

"We cannot teach every writing task that a doctoral student will encounter. Teaching therefore needs to help them understand how to approach an unfamiliar text type by developing rhetorical agility," says Peter Wingrove, a postdoctoral researcher at the Department of Communication and Learning in Science at Chalmers and lead author of the article published in the Journal of English for Academic Purposes .

In the study, the researchers trialed a teaching approach in which eight doctoral students worked with three different text genres during a single workshop. Participants first analyzed an academic abstract and discussed its intended audience, purpose and structure. They then worked in groups to turn a research blog post into an academic abstract and compared different ways of presenting the content.

Finally, they wrote an abstract of their own research and reworked it into a short popular science article. Participants were given examples to study, but no step-by-step guidance on how to complete the final task. The researchers analyzed participants' texts, recorded group discussions and conducted interviews about how they had approached the tasks.

The analysis showed how participants transferred both language and structure to the new writing task. Some placed key findings early in the text. Others used storytelling or questions to engage the reader. Participants also made different choices about technical terms in consideration of the new audience.

The interviews and group discussions also revealed how participants reasoned about their choices: which existing knowledge they could draw on, what needed to change and what they needed to learn more about. The researchers term the approach "Multi-Genre Pedagogy." Its aim is to develop flexible writing skills and a deeper awareness of genres by allowing participants to compare and move between different texts.

"Making research accessible can mean developing ideas in greater detail and explaining things that specialists take for granted. It is about understanding what readers need to follow the discussion," says Raffaella Negretti, professor at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

In a multi-genre workshop, eight doctoral students adapted research texts for academic and public audiences by changing structure, language and explanations. Analysis of texts, discussions and interviews indicated transfer of writing knowledge and awareness of audience needs, supporting multi-genre teaching for developing rhetorical flexibility.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
articles.dek: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.
paragraphs: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.

Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars.

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.
U. S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p. m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at:

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars. Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.”
NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates.
“The window is open. The mission is waiting. And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson.
The agency last opened applications in 2024. From more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are currently completing nearly two years of training.

“For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space. The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.”

Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions. The agency has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps, and selected applicants will join their ranks to study spacewalking, lunar geology, operations of high-performance aircraft, and more.

The basic requirements to apply include United States citizenship and a master’s degree in a STEM field, including engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution. The requirement for the master’s degree can also be met by:
Candidates must also have at least three years of related professional experience after completing their qualifying degree.

For medical doctors, residency training may count toward the professional experience requirement and must be completed by July 2027.

articles.title: Two paths, one flux: Trapped ions simulate Aharonov–Bohm interference in a lattice gauge theory
articles.dek: In a new Nature Physics study , researchers demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer.
paragraphs: In a new Nature Physics study , researchers demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer.

Gauge theories describe how matter interacts through fields called gauge fields, which carry the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces. They form the basis of the Standard Model of particle physics. In lattice gauge theories, space is modeled as a grid with matter at the vertices and gauge fields on the links connecting them.

Quantum simulators offer a way to study these theories. However, most quantum simulations of the simplest version—the Z₂ lattice gauge theory—have been limited to one spatial dimension, where effects linked to magnetic flux cannot appear.

To address this issue, researchers from the University of Oxford have now used trapped ions to simulate a Z₂ lattice gauge theory in a quasi-two-dimensional loop. The trapped ions perform a dual role. Their electronic states encode the gauge fields and their vibrations encode the matter.
Phys. org spoke to the first author of the study, Sebastian Saner, about the work.

"We first started brainstorming how to use a hybrid trapped-ion quantum system to simulate lattice gauge theories back in 2022. Later, during the project, we had the idea of using entangled qubits to encode the gauge-field flux. Coming up with this idea was one of the particularly exciting moments for us during the project," said Saner.
Using two trapped ions, the team built a closed loop to see how a flux stored in entangled qubits would affect a moving particle.

"Gauge theories describe how particles interact with each other through gauge fields. A simple example is two electrons repelling each other through the electromagnetic field," explained Saner. "In this picture, the electrons are described by a matter field, while the electromagnetic field is the gauge field that mediates their interaction."

Some of the most puzzling materials in physics, such as quantum spin liquids and high-temperature superconductors, are also described by gauge theories. Here, the gauge fields emerge from the collective behavior of electrons. Physicists often describe these materials using Z₂ lattice gauge theories, the simplest type, in which the field at each link of a grid can take only two values.
In these theories, the two values represent whether a field line is present or absent. Z₂ lattice gauge theories are also relevant to topological quantum error correction.

Simulating these theories on classical computers is challenging. According to Saner, computational complexity generally grows exponentially with system size, particularly in higher dimensions. The physics also becomes richer with each additional dimension.

For instance, in two spatial dimensions, links can form closed loops, which can be pierced by a magnetic flux. This gives rise to quasiparticles called visons, which have no counterpart in one dimension, where no loops can form.

Earlier experiments have studied Z₂ lattice gauge theories using cold atoms and superconducting qubits, but mostly in one-dimensional setups. Some experiments have simulated two-dimensional geometries, but removed the matter fields to simplify the model. As a result, these approaches could not capture how moving charges and gauge fields influence each other, including how flux affects particle motion.

articles.title: Earth's gravity may have kept the early moon's volcanic heart beating
articles.dek: We typically think of the moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an…
paragraphs: We typically think of the moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics—the moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4. 5 billion years ago. But some lunar material returned from the Chang'e-5 mission was notably formed only around 2 billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin.

So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than 2 billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, recently published in the journal Planet , offers an explanation—tidal heating.

Let's first set the stage of the moon's creation. Our best guess is that it was created when another early protoplanet, named Theia , slammed into Earth in a massive collision, creating a chunk of debris that coalesced into the moon. However, that amount of debris was relatively small—only about a quarter the size of the Earth itself, which meant the internal heat generated during its formation would rapidly radiate away, turning the moon itself geologically dormant.

But when Chang'e-5 returned some lunar basalts from Oceanus Procellarum back to Earth, laboratory dating showed them to be only around 2 billion years old. Basalts are only formed in active volcanoes or other environments with similarly high pressures and temperatures—environments that, at least according to traditional geological theory, shouldn't have existed on the moon 2 billion years ago.

Despite that, scientists have tried offering other solutions. Radioactive elements, such as potassium and uranium, emit some heat as they decay. But there wasn't enough undecayed material left on the moon to offer the amount of heat needed to form basalt 2 billion years ago. Asteroid strikes could cause localized high-impact thermal spikes, but the heavy bombardment period that gave the moon most of its craters had ended long before the basalt was formed.

So instead the authors turned to gravity—specifically to a phenomenon called tidal heating. This happens when a celestial body is squeezed, stretched and kneaded as it travels in an elliptical orbit around a larger parent body. Perhaps the most famous example of this in the solar system is Io. This moon of Jupiter is constantly erupting due to the tidal squishing it undergoes during its orbit around the largest planet.

Obviously, the moon doesn't seem to be undergoing any such squishing currently. However, 2 billion years ago, the moon was much closer to the Earth than it is today, orbiting our planet in 16 days rather than the 27 it takes now. Its orbit was also much more eccentric, looking much more like an oval than a circle. All of this means that Earth itself exerted huge rhythmic tidal forces on the moon's interior during the course of its orbit.

We've known that for a while, but astronomers have always modeled the moon as a mostly uniform sphere when trying to understand how these gravitational squeezes affected it. However, scientists knew this was a simplification—there is an ultra-low-viscosity zone of rock wrapping itself between the moon's core and mantle. When the research team plugged a more realistic 3D representation of the mantle setup into a convection simulation, they noticed that a ton of energy was directed specifically at two symmetric regions along the lunar core-mantle boundary.

These regions, which they named tidal heating anomaly zones (THAZs), absorbed a huge amount of energy. They calculated that, around 3. 2 billion years ago, despite taking up only 2. 5% of the mantle's total volume, the tidal strain on these regions delivered 150 gigawatts of power—more than four times the amount of energy generated by radioactive decay.

articles.title: Deep-Sea Scientists Capture Extraordinary 4K Footage of a Fish With a See-Through Head
articles.dek: MBARI’s first 4K footage of a barreleye fish offers a rare chance to study how its unusual eyes work in the ocean’s dim twilight zone.
paragraphs: MBARI’s first 4K footage of a barreleye fish offers a rare chance to study how its unusual eyes work in the ocean’s dim twilight zone.

The day’s deep-sea research was over when a fish with a transparent head came into view. Research Specialist Shannon Johnson spotted it as MBARI’s pilots were “flying” the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts back to the surface for recovery, and she called for them to stop.

The animal was a barreleye fish ( Macropinna microstoma ), approximately 600 meters (1,970 feet) underwater and 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore. For the MBARI scientists working aboard the research vessel David Packard , this was only the organization’s eleventh encounter with the species.

Senior Scientist Steven Haddock and researchers from MBARI’s Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were on the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition , studying gelatinous animals such as jellies, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. They combined scuba diving in open water near the surface with ROV surveys hundreds of meters below, filming and collecting animals to better understand how they have adapted to life in the deep water column.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship’s wet lab to prepare to catalog the specimens arriving with the ROV. When news of the barreleye reached them, they ran back to the control room. The encounter was an unexpected finish to a long, productive week of research.

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth,” said Haddock.

The team spent approximately 20 minutes observing the fish with Doc Ricketts ’ high-resolution 4K camera, examining its body and behavior and experimenting with different lighting conditions to show its transparent head shield. This was MBARI’s first barreleye sighting filmed in 4K and its first from the new flagship research vessel.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law also maneuvered Doc Ricketts close enough to record the fish with the vehicle’s virtual reality (VR) camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery could contribute to future education and outreach efforts.

MBARI has completed roughly 7,000 ROV dives and recorded more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video during nearly 40 years of ocean exploration. Its previous sighting of Macropinna was in 2021 . This summer, MBARI researchers leading an expedition with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another species of barreleye, the binocular fish ( Winteria telescopa ).

Earlier MBARI observations by Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped reveal how Macropinna uses its unusual eyes to feed. In the ocean’s dim twilight zone, the fish’s large fins keep it stable and allow it to maneuver as it hovers, looking upward for the silhouettes of prey. Once it spots food, its large, tubular eyes rotate beneath the transparent dome to keep the target in view. The gelatinous shield also protects those eyes when the fish plucks small crustaceans caught in the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores.

The researchers did not collect the barreleye, but their footage will support continued research on this elusive species. The Biodiversity and Biooptics Team studies how marine animals interact with light and has extensively investigated deep-sea visual systems. Its close-up examination of Macropinna ’s eyes will help researchers better understand vision in the twilight zone.

Pigments in the lenses of the fish’s eyes are thought to serve a similar function to the green pigments in the eyes of the strawberry squid ( Histioteuthis heteropsis ) , a deep-sea neighbor the team has previously studied.

“ Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” said Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

articles.title: Scientists discover new jellyfish species in waters off Alicante in Spain
articles.dek: The Mediterranean Sea still holds species unknown to science. One of them is Copula lucentia, a tiny jellyfish measuring just a few millimeters.
paragraphs: The Mediterranean Sea still holds species unknown to science. One of them is Copula lucentia, a tiny jellyfish measuring just a few millimeters. Discovered off El Campello, in Alicante, it was formally described in 2024 by a research team at the University of Alicante (UA) Marine Laboratory in Dénia, which forms part of the university's Ramón Margalef Multidisciplinary Institute for Environmental Research.

The finding makes Copula lucentia only the second box jellyfish species documented in the Mediterranean, following Carybdea marsupialis, described by Linnaeus in 1758. It shows that even one of the most thoroughly studied seas on the planet still has biodiversity to reveal.

Ranging from 1 to 7 millimeters (0. 04 to 0. 28 inches) in size, Copula lucentia was identified from specimens collected between 2016 and 2018. The description, published in the journal Marine Biodiversity in 2024, combined morphological studies with genetic analyses carried out in collaboration with international specialists.

Eva Fonfría, a researcher at the University of Alicante and lead author of the study, explained that the discovery was made during a sampling campaign. "At first we were surprised because it was very small for that time of year, and it had certain morphological features that didnt fit," she recalled.

These anomalies prompted the team to analyze the specimens and compare them with known species. The results confirmed that, although the organism belonged to the genus Copula, its distinctive features warranted classification as a new species.

The scientific name, Copula lucentia, refers to Lucentum, the Latin name for Alicante. To date, the species has been recorded only off El Campello, which makes this stretch of the Alicante coastline a key site for further research.

"Finding a new species in the Mediterranean, where everything is so heavily studied, is very important," said Fonfría, who stressed the need to continue studying these organisms in order to understand their distribution and ecological role in marine ecosystems.

Copula lucentia belongs to the box jellyfish group (Cubozoa), so called because of its cube-shaped bell. Its body is almost entirely transparent and has four tentacles, as well as small adhesive structures at the top that allow it to anchor itself to a variety of surfaces.
The specimens studied were found at depths of less than 1. 5 meters (4. 9 feet), in an environment of rocky and sandy seabeds and seagrass meadows.

Identifying the species required comparing several anatomical structures with those of Copula sivickisi, a related species found elsewhere in the world. Differences in the bell, together with genetic analysis, confirmed that the El Campello specimens belong to the same genus but constitute a distinct species.

According to César Bordehore, senior lecturer in the Department of Ecology at the University of Alicante and coordinator of the UA Marine Laboratory in Dénia, the discovery is a "milestone" for marine research. "The fact that we have identified a second box jellyfish species in the Mediterranean shows how much we still have to learn about its biodiversity," he said.
He also emphasized the need to expand research into small marine organisms, whose presence can easily go unnoticed.

Despite the progress that its identification represents, many questions about the new jellyfish remain unanswered. Its reproductive cycle, its role in the food web and its ability to sting all require further investigation. Bordehore noted that, more broadly, there is a need to better understand the role of gelatinous organisms in marine ecosystems—particularly small ones such as salps, tintinnids and jellyfish—which can interact significantly with key areas such as fisheries. These tiny organisms prey on fish eggs and larvae.

articles.title: Heavy rain can more than double glacier speeds in Alaska
articles.dek: Glaciers are often thought of as unyielding blocks of ice that slowly carve out the landscape as they move downhill by gravity.
paragraphs: Glaciers are often thought of as unyielding blocks of ice that slowly carve out the landscape as they move downhill by gravity. But sometimes their slow crawl becomes a surge that sees them move orders of magnitude faster than their usual speed.

Such events can have dramatic effects on the environment, acting like a bulldozer to erode valleys, shattering the glacier's surface into crevasses, blocking side valleys to create ice dams with temporary lakes behind, or causing catastrophic flooding when these ice dams burst. And as glaciers move toward the sea, increased ice calving and melting have considerable impacts on rising sea levels.

Understanding the mechanisms behind these aggressive advances is therefore vital for scientists to monitor instabilities in the world's glaciers and their wider implications for climate change conversations.
Parker Wilkerson, of Boise State University, and colleagues turned to the steep, highly crevassed Sít' Kusá (Turner Glacier) in Alaska to explore how rain can induce glacier surges.

Using GPS measurements from instruments installed around the glacier, the researchers recorded its position every 15 seconds to monitor speed changes in the short term compared to the glacier's longer-term movement. These were then associated with rain estimates validated by measurements taken at the weather station of the nearby Yakutat Airport to identify if there was a correlation between rainfall events and glacier surges. The results, published in The Cryosphere , show that there is.

Comparing a period of surge (2020–2021) to slow flow (2022–2024), the team found that over half of the rainfall events caused speed-ups, with the maximum reaching 7. 5 meters (24. 6 feet) in a single day—that's equivalent to a 116% increase in speed, or more than double.

This surge also lasted twice as long (66 hours) as any occurring during the quiescent flow period and tended to begin 12 hours after the start of the rainfall event when precipitation reached at least 20 mm (0. 79 inches). The glacier returned to a stable state three days later.

However, while rain-induced speed-ups were less frequent during quiescence, when they did occur, they required 60 mm (2. 4 inches) of rain since the start of the event and resulted in a much bigger percentage increase (251%) in speed, peaking on average 32 hours later. Despite this speed increase only being 1. 5 meters (4. 9 feet) per day, it is proportionately larger given the glacier is moving at such a slow background speed.

And during both phases, glacier acceleration was greatest in the downhill parts compared to those higher in the valley, likely a combination of landscape topography, gravity and meltwater aiding movement.

The researchers explain that the surge phenomenon is a consequence of the efficiency of the glacier's drainage system. An efficient one has linked channels running on top of, through and beneath the glacier that allow rainwater and meltwater to drain away quickly, meaning the glacier sits on the underlying bedrock and continues its slow, steady advance.

But an inefficient one creates issues. Water gets trapped in isolated pockets under the ice or in the sediment directly beneath the glacier (known as till) with nowhere to drain away. This causes pressure to build up as more water continues to enter these pockets and counteract the weight of the overlying ice, reducing friction and creating a lubricating layer for the glacier to slide quickly over the underlying ground.

Known as basal sliding, in other scenarios this can also be caused when the weight of ice reaches a critical point and the high pressure changes the temperature at which it melts to create a water layer between the glacier and bedrock.
These insights into the relationship between drainage efficiency and glacier speeds are vital for scientists to refine model projections for ice loss into the future.

Shifting weather patterns leading to more rain could be an important driving factor in the frequency and duration of surges in years to come. Coupled with increased melting in a warmer world, we are likely to see continued glacier ice loss and need to understand the implications of that for sea levels, especially for coastal and island communities at risk of flooding.

articles.title: The introduction of a medieval public health system exposed the population to roundworm
articles.dek: by Idun Haugan, Norwegian University of Science and Technology
paragraphs: by Idun Haugan, Norwegian University of Science and Technology
Medieval health and sanitation efforts involved deliberate interventions; however, some of these measures had the opposite effect, leading to an increased spread of disease in Trondheim.

Ancient skeletons from the city can tell us a great deal about how people lived, what they ate, what diseases they suffered from and what caused their deaths. They also provide insight into social conditions and how society was organized.

Inside the Trondheim Public Library, you can see parts of a medieval cemetery unearthed by archaeologists. This was the burial ground for people who belonged to a stone church that once stood beneath the library building.
Another medieval cemetery lies just across the street, situated beneath the premises of the current bank building, SpareBank 1.

One cemetery was centrally located in the oldest part of the city, while the other was situated on the outskirts of the urban core. Archaeological excavations and findings at these two sites have revealed significant differences between the individuals buried there.

Bone analysis indicates that child mortality was significantly higher, and general health poorer, among those buried in the cemetery on the city's periphery at the time—an area inhabited primarily by craft workers.

Their diet was less varied than that of Kaupmannastretet (known today as Krambugata) residents, who belonged to the church beneath the public library. The latter group represented the city's social elite; they were engaged in trade and resided in large townhouses. Their diet was more diverse, including seafood, for example. Social inequality affected health and mortality—then and today.
MedHeal600 ( Medieval Urban Health: From private to public responsibility ) is a research project led by the NTNU University Museum.
The researchers have investigated public health and living conditions in Trondheim from the year 1000 to 1600, including how public authorities facilitated access to health care.

Analyses of the skeletons reveal that well over half of the city's inhabitants experienced physiological stress during childhood and adolescence, caused by an insufficient or overly monotonous diet. Many people also died from infectious diseases such as leprosy, typhoid fever and tuberculosis.

"Society was familiar with these diseases, and public authorities implemented measures to limit their spread. In the Middle Ages, responsibility for health, hygiene and waste management shifted from being a private concern to increasingly becoming a public urban responsibility," says Axel Christophersen.
Christophersen is a professor emeritus of historical archaeology at the NTNU University Museum and has headed the Medieval Urban Health research project.
"The city initiated measures to improve hygiene, ensure cleaner streets and manage waste," says Christophersen.

articles.title: Scientists Find That Older Brains React Very Differently to a Night of Poor Sleep
articles.dek: A single bad night’s sleep may be easier on a healthy older brain than a younger one, though regularly missing sleep still carries risks.
paragraphs: A single bad night’s sleep may be easier on a healthy older brain than a younger one, though regularly missing sleep still carries risks.

Sleep quality often declines with age, yet older adults can seem less affected by a single bad night than younger people. Understanding that apparent mismatch means looking at how the brain responds when sleep runs short.

A study from Simon Fraser University offers a possible explanation. After just three hours of sleep, certain connections in younger and older brains changed in opposite directions. The findings suggest that healthy older brains may adapt to acute sleep loss in ways that help preserve function, although the study measured brain activity rather than cognitive performance.

The research, published in Imaging Neuroscience , compared brain networks in younger adults ages 20 to 30 with those in older adults ages 65 to 75. Lead researcher Josh Neudorf, an affiliate member of SFU’s Institute for Neuroscience and Neurotechnology, says earlier research on the effects of poor sleep provided a reason to investigate the difference.

“Older adults tend to better handle the effects of poor sleep, whereas younger adults, as we know, have the common symptoms of decreased mood and cognitive ability following poor sleep,” says Neudorf.
“This study tries to get at the heart of this difference – how does the older brain react to lost sleep.”

Brain connectivity describes how activity in different regions is linked. Stronger connections do not automatically mean the brain is working more efficiently. The arrangement matters, too. In a more modular network, regions are organized into groups, with relatively stronger connections within each group than between groups.
“What we found was quite striking in that older and younger brains actually responded in opposite ways to acute sleep loss.

“Certain connections in the brains of younger adults showed increased connectivity as a response to less sleep, while those same connections in the brains of older adults showed decreased connectivity.

“That decrease in connectivity promotes more efficient modular connectivity for the brain as a whole. In other words, the brain is acting in a more efficient way to maintain cognitive function. In contrast, the increased connectivity in younger brains suggests the brain is having to work harder to maintain function.”

Whether those network changes actually helped the older participants think or perform tasks better was not tested. The proposed benefit is an interpretation of the brain activity, consistent with previous research suggesting that older adults are often less impaired by a single night of poor sleep.

The reason for the opposite responses also remains open. One of several possible explanations is compensation, in which an aging brain reorganizes its networks and uses different strategies to maintain function.
“The quality of sleep starts to change and deteriorates somewhat in older adults,” says Neudorf.
“The theory of compensation is the idea that older brains adapt or compensate for those changes.”

articles.title: A Hidden Substance in Drinking Water May Be Linked to Heart Problems in Children
articles.dek: The water we drink may hold clues to a rare heart condition in children, but whether naturally occurring lithium plays a role in its development remains unknown.
paragraphs: The water we drink may hold clues to a rare heart condition in children, but whether naturally occurring lithium plays a role in its development remains unknown.

A dangerously fast heartbeat can begin with an extra strand of heart muscle that forms before birth. The strand creates an abnormal electrical connection, allowing the heart’s rhythm to go awry. Doctors can eliminate these connections, but a larger question has remained largely unanswered. Why do they develop in the first place?

A study led by UC San Francisco researchers points to a possible environmental clue in drinking water. Children living in areas with higher levels of naturally occurring lithium were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or WPW, a rare condition involving a particular type of abnormal connection. The findings, published online in The Journal of Clinical Investigation , show an association, but do not establish that lithium causes the condition.

These connections, known as accessory pathways, usually occur in people with no family history of the condition. That suggests environmental exposures during fetal development could play a role. Lithium attracted the researchers’ attention because medicinal doses taken during pregnancy have been associated with an increased risk of congenital heart defects, including Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare defect is frequently accompanied by accessory pathways, prompting the team to investigate whether lithium in drinking water might also be associated with changes in the developing heart.

The researchers analyzed health and water-quality data for more than 2. 3 million children in California. Just 686 had a documented WPW diagnosis. Children living in counties with lithium levels in the highest 25% had 71% greater odds of a diagnosis than those in counties with lower levels.

The team then tested its main finding among nearly 2 million children in New York. There, children living in areas with lithium levels above 10 parts per billion also had greater odds of a WPW diagnosis.

Higher lithium levels in California were also associated with palpitations, fainting, and supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT, a rapid heart rhythm that can cause palpitations and other symptoms. Accessory pathways are among the most common causes of SVT. WPW is also associated with a small increased risk of sudden death. Doctors can treat accessory pathways with catheter ablation, a minimally invasive procedure that eliminates the small area of heart tissue responsible for the abnormal electrical connection.

“We’ve known about these pathways for decades, and we know how to treat them, but we haven’t known why people develop them,” said Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, an endowed professor in atrial fibrillation research in the UCSF Division of Cardiology and senior author of the study. “This is an exciting step because it points to a potential environmental factor that may be modifiable. But we need more research to determine whether lithium is actually contributing to their development.”

The study estimated exposure from the county of residence. Researchers did not know how much lithium individual children or their mothers consumed, and other environmental or genetic factors could help explain the association. Studies in other populations and research that measures exposure during pregnancy more precisely are needed to determine whether lithium plays a causal role.
Marcus said the findings should not alarm people about the safety of their drinking water, including those who are pregnant. Despite the association, WPW was rare in the children studied.

Lithium occurs naturally in groundwater, and its concentration varies widely by location. Groundwater used for drinking water across the United States and elsewhere contains lithium, raising questions about the findings’ potential public health significance beyond California and New York. The researchers said the results underscore the value of collecting environmental data to understand how ordinary exposures may affect health.

“We’re exposed to things in our environment every day, including substances that occur naturally,” Marcus said. “The more precisely we can measure those exposures and connect them with health outcomes, the better we can understand what may be influencing health.”

Lithium in drinking water is not currently regulated in the United States, although the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency requires monitoring through its program for unregulated contaminants. The U. S. Geological Survey also measures lithium in groundwater.

articles.title: Scientists Find a Clever Way to Read Quantum Information Without Destroying It
articles.dek: Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and…
paragraphs: Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and fewer components.

Like a bit in an ordinary computer, a qubit stores information using states labeled 0 and 1. A qubit can also be prepared in a superposition, a quantum combination of the two. These states belong to a physical system that researchers build and control. In the design explored here, that system is a tiny wire connected to superconducting materials.

The aim of quantum computing is to use quantum behavior to perform certain calculations more efficiently than conventional computers. That requires control: researchers must prepare qubits and change their states deliberately. Unwanted interactions with the surroundings can disrupt them, and measuring a qubit can alter it, too.

A theoretical study proposes reading one type of qubit through an electric current it produces itself. This could let researchers follow its behavior with minimal disturbance and without the extra qubits used in many existing methods.

Andreev qubits hold information in states formed between superconducting materials, which carry electric current without resistance. They are named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who described the underlying process at the boundary between normal and superconducting materials in 1964.

“In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined – formed in an indium arsenide [ InAs ] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It’s in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed,” explains José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil.

“In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained,” says Egues.

Many existing methods use a helper quantum system called an ancilla. Researchers prepare it, connect it to the qubit, transfer information to it, and measure it to preserve the original qubit as much as possible. These steps add time and equipment. “Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself,” says Egues.

The qubit would sit in a closed superconducting circuit carrying a supercurrent, an electric current that flows without resistance. The calculations predict that interference between the states in the qubit’s superposition makes part of this current oscillate. “It’s precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It’s that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal,” Egues points out.

An applied voltage usually causes this kind of oscillation, known as the AC Josephson effect. “Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It’s the very evolution of the qubit’s state that produces that oscillation,” says Egues.

A nearby superconducting quantum interference device, or SQUID, would act as the detector. These instruments are extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields. Egues explains, “We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID ‘senses’ that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”
Identifying the qubit’s state requires knowing both the balance of 0 and 1 and their relative phase, or how the two components line up.

“Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it’s possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit,” Egues explains.
Researchers could also track the qubit through repeated readings without resetting it to its initial state after each measurement.

articles.title: Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology
articles.dek: Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries.
paragraphs: Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82. 3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43. 0% for batteries using untreated lithium.

The researchers at Xidian University developed a simple liquid coating that reacts with lithium metal to form a protective barrier. Their findings, published in Science China Chemistry , suggest a possible route toward safer, more durable batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.

Lithium metal has been called the “holy grail” of energy storage because it can theoretically store nearly ten times as much charge per gram as the graphite used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Its exceptional capacity could enable lighter batteries that store more energy and potentially support longer driving ranges.

To address this problem, researchers led by Professors Siwu Li, Weiwei Wu, and Chuang Yu combined a silicon-based polymer with indium chloride. When applied to lithium, the mixture forms lithium fluoride and lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles within a flexible protective film just 12 micrometers thick (about 0. 00047 inches).

“This hybrid layer acts like a smart fortress,” explains corresponding author Siwu Li. “The polymer backbone provides flexibility to absorb the mechanical stress of lithium expanding and contracting. The lithium fluoride phase blocks electrons to prevent dendrite nucleation. And the lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles act as traffic conductors, guiding lithium ions to deposit evenly rather than piling up in dangerous spikes.”

The coated lithium electrodes withstood a critical current density of 3. 5 milliamperes per square centimeter, more than four times the 0. 8 achieved by untreated lithium. In complete batteries containing a nickel-cobalt-manganese oxide cathode and a sulfide solid electrolyte, the protected electrodes delivered an initial capacity of 129. 8 milliampere-hours per gram and retained 82. 3% after 300 cycles at 0. 5C.
Spectroscopy and electron microscopy confirmed the coating’s composition and revealed a dense, uniform layer without visible cracks or gaps.
The coating could help address the chemical instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes, a major challenge in solid-state battery development.

Because the protective layer forms from an applied liquid, it may be compatible with existing industrial coating equipment without requiring expensive vacuum processing. The researchers also plan to explore alternatives to indium, including tin and zinc.
Although commercial performance remains unproven, the findings offer a promising approach to making high-energy lithium metal batteries more stable and longer-lasting.

articles.title: Kids Who Learn To Swim Early May Have an Unexpected Advantage in School
articles.dek: Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.
paragraphs: Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.

When family budgets tighten, swimming lessons can be among the first expenses to go. Most swim schools operate as commercial businesses, and cost is the biggest barrier to participation. Yet the consequences of missing out may extend beyond water safety and fitness to the skills children need when they start school.

A four-year study involving nearly 7,000 survey respondents and individual testing of 177 children suggests that children who learn to swim early have developmental advantages over their peers. Participants younger than 5 could be 5 to 18 months ahead of typical milestones in literacy, numeracy, and following instructions compared with the general population of children their age. Those advantages remained when socioeconomic background was taken into account.
Robyn Jorgensen, Emeritus Professor at the University of Canberra in Australia, examines and expands on the research in her new book, Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim .

Jorgensen does not interpret the findings as evidence that children who learn to swim are innately smarter. Instead, she argues that lessons develop skills and habits children can carry into the classroom. A child counting kicks from one to ten with an instructor, for example, is practicing number sequencing and one-to-one correspondence, matching each number to a single action.

The project grew out of a conversation between Jorgensen and Laurie Lawrence, an Olympic swim coach inducted into both the Australian and U. S. Swimming Halls of Fame. Lawrence thought children who learned to swim early generally seemed more “school-ready.”
“There was no formal evidence to support this observation, but it was one that Laurie felt he and many others in the swim industry observed,” Jorgensen explains.

To investigate that “industry hunch,” Jorgensen and her colleagues used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments. These internationally recognized testing tools were normed against national census data, providing reference standards for comparing the children’s performance with that of the wider population.

The results surprised even Jorgensen, who said, “My early observations of the young learners piqued my interest while retaining some sense of skepticism about what could be achieved. I am not from a swimming background, so had no vested interest in the ‘proving’ or otherwise of Laurie’s hunch. My only interest in swimming was as a grandparent and around water safety for my children and grandchildren, and as a recreational activity.”

Beyond the literacy and numeracy findings, the research suggests that early swimming participants are more sociable and have measurable advantages in cognitive development, language skills, and emotional regulation. These findings point to potential benefits for academic success.
“It is reasonable to claim that swimming prepares children for the schooling years, particularly the early years and the transition into schooling,” Jorgensen explains.

Access to those potential benefits is sharply unequal. Jorgensen’s analysis identifies the United States and China as having the greatest inequities in access, with regular swimming lessons affordable only to very affluent families. Singapore, Australia, Brazil, and South Africa also face substantial economic and geographic barriers.

One respondent from Zimbabwe described how lessons compete with basic necessities. “So swimming is still seen in Africa in general as elite. But basically, if you are a working-level person well below average, swimming lessons will not be a priority; what will be a priority is feeding your family.”

Even reaching a pool can be difficult. In Australia, families on remote farming properties can face journeys of hundreds of kilometers to the nearest one. The study describes “a double whammy” for children from low-income and rural communities, who are both the least likely to have access to lessons and the most at risk of drowning.

articles.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
articles.dek: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U. S. -supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.
The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U. S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

articles.title: Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results
articles.dek: In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered…
paragraphs: In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.

For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?

A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.

Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6. 5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The findings were published in Diabetes Care , a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M. D. , MPH, Sc. D. , of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.

Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.

Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.

The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph. D. , was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”

Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.

“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph. D. , Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”
